messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Network Engineer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Stop Enjoyment: give up pleasant activities, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Mele was 66 when she came for treatment, a widowed network engineer who had spent decades building a reputation for steadiness, precision, and calm problem-solving. She described the assault in a matter-of-fact voice at first, but the moments that stayed sharpest for her were sensory and interpersonal. It happened after an evening work function where alcohol had been flowing, at a point in her life when she had expected to be beyond this kind of danger, not newly vulnerable to it. She had stayed later than she meant to, talking with colleagues and trying to be sociable in a way that had once felt ordinary. When she was leaving, a man she knew approached her with the easy familiarity of someone stepping too close, the smell of alcohol heavy on him. She remembered trying to keep the interaction polite, not wanting to make a scene. What frightened her most now was not only that he ignored her boundaries, but that he moved into the space of affection and closeness as if he were entitled to it. His hands were on her before she could fully register what was happening. She remembered freezing, feeling his nearness and the alcohol on his breath, and afterward being sickened by the thought that in those moments she had not fought in the way she believed she should have. At 66, she found herself appalled that she still replayed the encounter in terms of what she “should” have done, as if age and competence ought to have protected her; she had come to believe that she had acted in ways that went against who she was, and she carried a lasting shame about what had happened to her body.

In the months afterward, the world narrowed around very specific moments. Hugs became intolerable. Even gestures other people meant as warmth or comfort made her body seize with alarm. At work, when a colleague leaned in to congratulate her on solving a network outage and reached to touch her arm, she jerked back before she could think, heart pounding, scanning the desk beside her for anything sharp or heavy. She noticed herself doing that everywhere: in conference rooms, restaurants, parking garages, even in friends’ kitchens. Her eyes would go immediately to scissors, letter openers, glass bottles, heavy lamps, anything that could become a weapon. Other people would reassure her that she was safe, that nothing was happening, but the reassurance never landed. She was certain safety could disappear in an instant, and that being told otherwise only showed how little other people understood. The smell of alcohol was one of the fastest ways she could be pulled into that state. A coworker returning from a client dinner, a stranger passing too close in an elevator, the stale scent outside a bar when she walked from the office to her car—each could make her stomach drop and her muscles tense.

Emotional closeness became dangerous too. If someone asked too many caring questions or tried to sit with her grief as a widow and now as someone clearly struggling, she felt cornered. She began declining invitations from the small circle of friends who had tried to stay close after her husband died. When one longtime friend opened her arms for a goodbye hug, Mele stepped back so abruptly that both of them went quiet. After that, she kept conversations brief and practical. She told herself it was better not to let people in, because closeness made her vulnerable in ways she no longer believed she could protect against. Her attempts to regain control settled into rigid habits. Eating became one of the few areas where she felt she could impose order. She restricted herself strictly, taking a grim satisfaction in rules about portions and timing, as though discipline might hold back the sense that bad things could happen to her without warning. She also gave up things that had once brought relief or pleasure. She stopped meeting friends for meals, stopped going to the seaside path she used to walk on weekends, stopped allowing herself small enjoyments she would once have considered harmless.

Life became work, errands, and being home alone. The cost showed up in concrete ways. At the office, younger staff had started to experience her as distant and unapproachable, and she withdrew from mentoring tasks she had once done generously. Outside work, her isolation deepened; she was widowed already, and now she was cutting herself off from the few remaining forms of comfort and companionship available to her. By the time she sought help, Mele was exhausted by living in a body that startled at unexpected touch and a mind that never stopped calculating danger. The immediate push came after a routine moment at work: a teammate approached from behind during a server-room problem, touched her shoulder to get her attention, and she spun around in panic, knocking a tool tray to the floor. She was humiliated by how quickly she had gone from concentration to terror, and by how exposed she felt when people stared.

In therapy she said she was tired of arranging her whole life around avoiding closeness, alcohol smells, and any situation where someone might reach for her. She spoke as a 66-year-old woman who felt her life had become much smaller than she ever imagined it would be at this stage, reduced to vigilance, rules, and distance. At the same time, she was afraid that if she let down her guard even slightly, it would prove what she already believed—that she could not stop bad things from happening. What she hoped for, cautiously, was not to become carefree, but to be able to be near people again without feeling that her body and her values had both been permanently broken.
